name: Gore-Tex lip implant (SoftForm)

lead: Gore-Tex lip implants are thin strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) placed in the lip to add permanent volume. The fuller lip is visible after healing.

Wikipedia lists SoftForm, Advanta and UltraSoft as commercial versions, in diameters of 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm. ePTFE is a long-established implant and graft material in vascular, cardiac, hernia and facial plastic surgery. The sources reviewed describe the lip use only briefly, and no clinical studies specific to lip use were found.

paras: A surgeon inserts a solid or hollow ePTFE tube into the lip tissue, where it physically occupies space and increases lip volume. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, it is a physical device rather than an injectable.
Wikipedia lists implant movement and extrusion (breaking through the tissue) among complications of lip implants, along with bleeding, asymmetry and lumpiness.

chain: Tube of ePTFE placed in lip
angle.text: A thin tube of Gore-Tex-type ePTFE is placed in the lip for permanent added volume, sold under names such as Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm. The fuller lip is visible after healing. Sources describe it briefly, and implant movement and extrusion are listed complications.

lead: Gore-Tex lip implants are strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) that a surgeon places in the lip to add permanent volume and definition, an option for people who want fuller lips from a solid implant instead of repeated injectable fillers. Wikipedia describes them as 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm in diameter and names Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm as commercial versions.[1]

ePTFE is also used as a graft and implant material in vascular, cardiac, hernia and facial plastic surgery.[2] The SoftForm implant was developed for facial soft-tissue augmentation, and a 2000 historical review in Facial Plastic Surgery described it as a subcutaneous implant created for deep nasolabial folds and other facial furrows.[3]

Published surgeon series on perioral ePTFE implants include a review of 175 SoftForm pieces placed in 69 patients and 106 Advanta implants in 42 patients, which reported shrinkage and migration with low-porosity implants and described a dual-porosity design,[4] and a patient-satisfaction survey of 50 patients who received SoftForm in the perioral region, including the upper and lower lip.[5]

paras: Lip implants made of Gore-Tex are delivered as strips or tubes and sold under names including SoftForm.[1] Wikipedia presents them among several lip augmentation options that also include fillers, fat transfer, donor tissue and surgical flaps.[1]

Facial plastic surgery literature groups SoftForm with implants used in the nasolabial fold, melomental fold and lips, and a 2002 paper describes a technique and a dedicated instrument for inserting dual-porosity ePTFE implants.[3][4][5]

A 2002 paper in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery reported on 175 pieces of SoftForm (Collagen Corporation) placed in 69 patients over three years, plus 106 Advanta implants (Atrium Medical) in 42 patients between 1997 and 2000.[4] The author reported significant problems with shrinkage and migration of low-porosity ePTFE implants and preliminarily described a dual-porosity implant as offering a lower incidence of these complications and as subjectively softer once in place.[4]

A 2003 retrospective telephone survey in the same journal followed 38 of 50 patients (76 percent) who had Softform implants to the melolabial fold, melomental fold, upper lip and lower lip, at a mean of 22.7 months after the procedure, to assess satisfaction.[5]

Wikipedia lists implant-specific complications of lip augmentation as movement of the implant and extrusion through the tissue, and more general ones including bleeding, uneven lips and lumpiness.[1] The 2002 series reported shrinkage and migration with low-porosity implants.[4]

Two surgeon-reported studies examined SoftForm and related ePTFE implants in the perioral region: a case review of 175 SoftForm and 106 Advanta implants that described shrinkage and migration with low-porosity designs, and a 50-patient retrospective satisfaction survey.[4][5] A 2000 historical review covers the development and techniques of SoftForm for facial rejuvenation.[3]

timeline.event: Start of a three-year series of Advanta ePTFE implant placements later reported in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery.[4]
Facial Plastic Surgery publishes a historical review of SoftForm for facial rejuvenation.[3]
A paper reports shrinkage and migration with low-porosity ePTFE implants and describes a dual-porosity design.[4]
A patient-satisfaction survey of SoftForm perioral implants is published.[5]
